You should try the following : check your connection, disable ad-blocker, clear your browser cache, try in private mode, try from another browser/computer/connection. 0 Brass: Lancashire Brass: Lancashire — first published as Brass — is an economic strategy game that tells the story of competing cotton entrepreneurs in Lancashire during the industrial revolution. You must develop, build and establish your industries and network so that you can capitalize on demand for iron, coal and cotton. The game is played over two halves: the canal phase and the rail phase. To win the game, score the most victory points (VPs), which are counted at the end of each phase. VPs are gained from your canals, rails, and established (flipped) industry tiles. Each round, players take turns according to the turn order track, receiving two actions to perform any of the following: build an industry tile, build a rail or canal, develop an industry, sell cotton, take a loan At the end of your turn, you replace the two cards you played with two more from the deck. Turn order is determined by how much money a player spent on the previous turn, the lowest spender going first. This turn order mechanism opens some strategic options for players going later in the turn order, allowing for the possibility of back-to-back turns. After all the cards have been played the first time (with the deck size being adjusted for the number of players), the canal phase ends and a scoring round commences. After scoring, all canals and all of the lowest level industries are removed from the game, after which new cards are dealt and the rail phase begins. During this phase, players may now occupy more than one location in a city and double-connection builds (though expensive) are possible. At the end of the rail phase, another scoring round takes place, then a winner is crowned. The cards limit where you can build your industries, sell cotton or build connections (though any card can be used to 'develop'). This leads to a strategic timing/storing of cards. Resources are common so that if you build a rail line (which requires coal) you have to use the coal from the nearest source, which may be an opponent's coal mine, which in turn gets that coal mine closer to scoring (i.e., being utilized). [Rating: 1/10] Really stuffy and boring game. Just takes hours to play. FRules have some flaws. Much exceptions in the rules.

[Rating: 1/10] Nothing wrong with game. I'm sure its a splendid affair. However after watching run through and or reading reviews, absolutely no desire to play.

[Rating: 1/10] I had fun with my play but didn't really see the magic, don't know if I had enough fun to put in the reps to get it though.

[Rating: 1/10] Excellent economic euro with a wealth of depth and strategy to it. The card play keeps it fresh on repeated play while not being random enough to prevent consistent strategies. Overall a much better game than Birmingham at exactly 4 players but unfortunately doesn't scale as well with lower player counts. I'd say time hasn't been kind to Brass, but there are many older economic games that are better that in hindsight this was never anything special even when it first came out.

[Rating: 1/10] My suspicion is that people love this just because there's an income tracker and WHEE they get stuff automatically. Even though the income is usually a trap. I kinda get why the random demand tokens are in as a mechanic, but the theme is completely backwards with people flipping them first. And the ships just do nothing?  The rules are kind of a mess, and the game mostly rewards railroad-building in era 2 anyway. It's more of a quick train game first, with a long goods-selling phase that isn't nearly as profitable.
